text: Jules François Camille Ferry (French: [ʒyl fɛʁi]; 5 April 1832 – 17 March 1893) was a French statesman and republican philosopher who led the Moderate Republicans and served as Prime Minister of France from 1880 to 1881 and 1883 to 1885. He was a strong advocate of laicism and colonial expansion. Under the Third Republic, Ferry implemented laws that made primary education in France free, non-clerical (laïque), and compulsory. He reorganized the committee of public education through a law of 27 February 1880 and proposed regulations for university degrees, which sparked controversy due to Article 7 removing teaching rights from unauthorized religious orders. He successfully passed his eponymous laws of 16 June 1881 and 28 March 1882, establishing free, laical, and mandatory primary education. In higher education, the number of professors known as the "Republic's black hussars" doubled under his ministry. After France’s defeat by Prussia in 1870, Ferry promoted colonial expansion primarily for economic gain. In 1882, as Minister of Public Instruction, he launched a scientific exploration mission to Tunisia, led by botanist Ernest Cosson and including Napoléon Doumet-Adanson, with a geological section under Georges Rolland added in 1884, assisted by Philippe Thomas from 1885 and Georges Le Mesle in 1887. In a speech before the Chamber of Deputies on 28 March 1884, he stated that "it is a right for the superior races, because they have a duty. They have the duty to civilize the inferior races." He directed negotiations leading to a French protectorate in Tunis (1881), prepared the treaty of 17 December 1885 for the occupation of Madagascar, organized the conquest of Annam and Tonkin (Indochina), and initiated exploration in the Congo and Niger regions. The war with the Qing dynasty over these territories, triggered by the French retreat from Lạng Sơn, led to the Tonkin Affair, resulting in violent criticism from Clemenceau and other radicals, and Ferry’s resignation on 30 March 1885. Although the peace treaty of 9 June 1885, in which the Qing ceded suzerainty over Annam and Tonkin to France, was negotiated under his ministry, he never again served as premier. Ferry opposed monarchy, having witnessed Henri, Count of Chambord’s early bid, and conducted a widespread purge of monarchists from key state positions. In the 1890s, he visited Algeria and warned that a conflict between Indigènes and Europeans was inevitable. Ferry held the longest tenure as Prime Minister under the Third Republic until Georges Clemenceau became premier twice in the 20th century. He believed France should avoid confrontation with Wilhelmine Germany, favoring cooperation with Otto von Bismarck over threats of future war, a pragmatic but unpopular stance. Bismarck, though initially wary, accepted Ferry’s approach, supported French colonial expansion, and proposed Franco-German cooperation against the British Empire, leading to a colonial rivalry in Africa that nearly escalated into war at Fashoda in 1898—though both leaders died before the conflict materialized. The rivalry eventually led to the Entente Cordiale in 1904. Ferry remained a key figure in the moderate republican party and opposed General Boulanger. After Jules Grévy’s resignation on 2 December 1887, Ferry ran for president but was rejected by radicals and withdrew in favor of Sadi Carnot. On 10 December 1887, a man named Aubertin attempted to assassinate Ferry, who died on 17 March 1893 from complications of the wound. The Chamber of Deputies granted him a state funeral.
